titel: Basics of US investment income taxes
kurz: How the federal government taxes interest, dividends and capital gains at different rates, what the 3.8% net investment income tax adds, and why no one withholds the tax for you.

bloecke.md:
The United States has no separate flat tax on investment income. Interest, dividends and capital gains are part of the federal income tax and are reported on the same Form 1040 as wages. What differs is the rate. Most investment income is taxed as ordinary income at the regular rates of 10% to 37%. Two kinds of income receive preferential rates of 0%, 15% or 20%: long-term capital gains and qualified dividends (26 U.S.C. § 1(h)).

The preferential treatment of capital gains is old; a lower rate for gains on assets held for more than two years was introduced as early as 1921. The current structure goes back to two later laws. The Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2003 lowered the top rate on long-term gains to 15% and for the first time extended it to qualified dividends. The American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 made this permanent and added a 20% rate for the highest incomes. Since 2013, the net investment income tax of 3.8% (26 U.S.C. § 1411), introduced to help finance the Affordable Care Act, has applied on top for high earners.

The key difference from wage income is therefore not a special tax but a special rate schedule. Whether $1,000 of investment income costs you $0, $150, $220 or more depends on what kind of income it is, how long you held the asset and how high the rest of your taxable income is.

bloecke.md:
## Kinds of investment income

- **Interest** from savings accounts, CDs, bonds and money market funds is ordinary income. Interest on US Treasury securities is exempt from state and local income tax, and interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax.
- **Dividends** are ordinary unless they are qualified. A dividend is qualified if it comes from a US corporation or a qualifying foreign corporation and you held the stock for more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date. Dividends from REITs and from bond funds are generally not qualified.
- **Capital gains** arise when you sell an asset for more than its basis. If you held it for one year or less, the gain is short-term and taxed as ordinary income. If you held it for more than one year, it is long-term and qualifies for the 0%, 15% or 20% rates.

Some capital assets follow their own rules. Long-term gains on collectibles, which include physical gold and many gold funds structured as grantor trusts, are taxed at up to 28%. Rental income is not investment income in this sense; it is reported on Schedule E and taxed at ordinary rates. Cryptoassets are treated as property, so selling them produces capital gains or losses.

## Tax base

On a sale, the gain is the amount realized minus your adjusted basis. The basis is usually what you paid, including commissions and other purchase costs; selling costs reduce the amount realized. Reinvested dividends buy new shares and add to your basis, which matters later when you sell.

Other costs generally do not reduce your tax. Advisory fees, custody fees, newsletters and subscriptions were miscellaneous itemized deductions, which have been suspended since 2018; the 2025 budget law (Public Law 119-21) made this permanent. Interest on money borrowed to buy taxable investments can still be deducted as investment interest expense if you itemize (Form 4952). For most investors, however, there is no deduction for investment expenses at all.

You buy 100 shares at $40.00 through a commission-free broker. Your basis is $4,000.00.

Three years later, you sell the 100 shares at $55.00, for $5,500.00.

The gain is 5,500.00 − 4,000.00 = $1,500.00. Because you held the shares for more than one year, it is a long-term capital gain.

As a single filer with $80,000 of taxable income in 2026, you pay 15%, or $225.00. Had you sold after eleven months, the same gain would be short-term and taxed at your ordinary rate of 22%, or $330.00. One month of extra patience is worth $105.00 here.

bloecke.formel: Tax on preferential income = 0% × A + 15% × B + 20% × C
bloecke.erklaerung: Long-term gains and qualified dividends are stacked on top of your ordinary taxable income. A is the part that falls below the 0% threshold, B the part between the 0% and 15% thresholds, and C the part above. Ordinary income fills the brackets first, so the more wages you have, the less room is left at 0%. Preferential income never pushes your ordinary income into a higher bracket.

bloecke.md: The NIIT of 3.8% applies to the smaller of your net investment income and the amount by which your modified adjusted gross income exceeds $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (married filing jointly). Interest, dividends, capital gains and passive rental income count; tax-exempt municipal bond interest and withdrawals from retirement accounts do not. The thresholds are fixed in the statute and have not been adjusted for inflation since 2013, so every year more households cross them.

## Who collects the tax

For US persons, there is normally no withholding on interest, dividends or capital gains. Your broker or bank credits the full amount and reports it to you and to the IRS on Form 1099-INT, 1099-DIV and 1099-B, usually as a consolidated statement by mid-February. You report the income on your return: interest and dividends on Form 1040 and, above $1,500, on Schedule B; each sale on Form 8949, summarized on Schedule D.

Because nothing is withheld, the tax has to be paid during the year. The IRS expects quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES, due in April, June, September and January) or enough withholding from wages. You generally avoid an underpayment penalty if you pay at least 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax, or 110% if your adjusted gross income was above $150,000.

The exception is **backup withholding**. If the broker does not have a correct taxpayer identification number certified on Form W-9, it must withhold 24% of dividends, interest and sale proceeds. This is credited on your return, but it is avoidable.

bloecke.unter: For US persons, the broker usually reports but does not withhold. The tax is settled through estimated payments and your return.

bloecke.titel: What happens when income is missing from the return
bloecke.md:
The IRS compares every Form 1099 it receives with your return. If income is missing, it sends a CP2000 notice proposing the additional tax plus interest and, often, an accuracy-related penalty of 20% of the underpayment.

- A late or corrected 1099 is common for funds and brokers, often in March. Filing very early increases the risk of having to amend.
- If the 1099-B says the basis was not reported to the IRS, you must enter it yourself on Form 8949. If you leave it blank, the full proceeds look like gain.
- Income from foreign accounts is taxable even if no 1099 is issued. US citizens and residents are taxed on worldwide income, and foreign accounts may also have to be reported on the FBAR and Form 8938.

## Taxation of nominal income

The federal tax makes no adjustment for inflation. The basis of an asset is not indexed, and interest is taxed in full even when it only offsets the loss of purchasing power. A 4% savings rate in a year with 3% inflation is a real return of about 1% before tax, but the tax is calculated on all 4%.

This gives a rule of thumb. With a marginal rate t on interest, the nominal rate must be at least inflation ÷ (1 − t) to preserve purchasing power after tax. In the 22% bracket and with 3% inflation, that is 3.85%. State income tax raises the threshold further. Long-term gains suffer less from this because the rate is lower and the tax is only due when you sell.

bloecke.unter: Assumed inflation of 3%. In the 22% bracket, the threshold for preserving purchasing power after federal tax is a nominal rate of about 3.85%; without tax, it is 3%.

bloecke.md:
1. Keep your Form W-9 current. A wrong name or number leads to 24% backup withholding.
2. Read the 1099-B line by line. Check that each sale is marked short-term or long-term correctly and that the basis is filled in, especially for shares bought before 2011 or transferred from another broker.
3. Plan your estimated payments. A large gain in May is due with the June payment, not in April of the following year; the safe-harbor rules tell you how much is enough.

The federal income tax taxes most kinds of income on one progressive schedule. Long-term gains and qualified dividends are an exception: a single filer with $80,000 of taxable income pays 22% on the next dollar of wages but only 15% on the next dollar of long-term gain.

Three arguments are usually made for this. The first is double taxation: corporate profits are taxed at the corporate level, since 2018 at 21%, before they are paid out as dividends or reflected in the share price. The second is inflation: because basis is not indexed, part of every long-term gain is not a real gain. The third is the lock-in effect: a high tax on realization discourages investors from selling and reallocating capital.

The counter-argument is that the benefit flows mainly to households with high incomes, whose income consists largely of capital gains, so that the average tax rate can be lower for them than for many wage earners. How capital income should be taxed remains politically contested. This lesson describes the law as of 2026.

mitnehmen: Interest, short-term gains and nonqualified dividends are taxed as ordinary income at 10% to 37%; long-term gains and qualified dividends at 0%, 15% or 20%.
Long-term means held for more than one year; the preferential income is stacked on top of ordinary income, which decides how much of it falls into the 0% range.
Above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (joint) of modified adjusted gross income, the 3.8% net investment income tax is added, and most states tax investment income too.
Brokers report on Forms 1099 but usually withhold nothing; you pay through estimated payments or wage withholding and settle on Form 1040.
The tax is levied on nominal income; in the 22% bracket and at 3% inflation, interest must reach about 3.85% just to preserve purchasing power.

begriffe.text: Gain on a capital asset held for more than one year. Taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on taxable income (26 U.S.C. § 1(h)); gains on assets held one year or less are short-term and taxed as ordinary income.

Dividend from a US or qualifying foreign corporation on stock held for more than 60 days in the 121-day period around the ex-dividend date. Taxed at the same rates as long-term capital gains; reported in box 1b of Form 1099-DIV.

Additional federal tax of 3.8% on net investment income above fixed thresholds of modified adjusted gross income ($200,000 single, $250,000 married filing jointly), in force since 2013 (26 U.S.C. § 1411).
What an asset cost you, including purchase costs and reinvested dividends, adjusted for items such as return of capital. Gain or loss on a sale is the amount realized minus the adjusted basis.

Withholding of 24% that a payer must apply to dividends, interest and sale proceeds if it lacks a correct, certified taxpayer identification number (Form W-9) or the IRS has instructed it to withhold.
